blocks.text: 1. Learning Rate Scheduling

blocks.alt: Learning rate changes over epochs following a schedule

blocks.text: Every optimizer covered throughout this entire module, from plain Stochastic Gradient Descent through Nadam, relies on a learning rate to determine how large each individual update step actually is. Learning Rate Scheduling asks a genuinely different question: should that rate actually stay fixed throughout the entire training run?

It is the final topic of this module, applicable on top of essentially any optimizer already covered, a genuinely orthogonal enhancement rather than a replacement for anything covered in the earlier topics of this module.
2. The Limitation of a Fixed Rate

blocks.alt: A fixed learning rate is wrong for some phase of training

blocks.text: A genuine tension every fixed learning rate faces is real and unavoidable. Too large, held constant throughout the entire training run, can genuinely prevent fine, precise convergence near the actual minimum, particularly late in training when small, careful adjustments actually matter most.

Too small, held constant throughout instead, produces genuinely slow progress, especially early in training, when faster, larger movement would actually help considerably more, before the network has settled anywhere near its eventual, final solution.
3. The Scheduling Idea

This connects back to the fixed-rate tension already covered in the previous section. The core scheduling idea starts training with a genuinely larger learning rate, then gradually reduces it as training actually progresses.

This produces fast, coarse progress early in training, when a large learning rate genuinely helps, followed by fine, precise refinement late in training, when a genuinely smaller learning rate becomes considerably more appropriate, directly resolving the tension already covered above.

blocks.text: 4. Step Decay

blocks.alt: The learning rate drops at fixed points

blocks.text: A genuinely common, simple scheduling approach is step decay, reducing the learning rate by a fixed factor, every fixed number of epochs, cutting it in half every 10 epochs for instance.
This produces a genuinely simple, easy-to-implement schedule with clear, discrete drop points, making it straightforward to reason about and to actually monitor during a real, ongoing training run.
5. Exponential Decay

blocks.alt: The learning rate shrinks exponentially every step

blocks.text: Another genuinely common approach is exponential decay, reducing the learning rate smoothly, continuously, epoch by epoch, rather than in the sudden, discrete jumps step decay, already covered in the previous section, actually uses.
This produces a genuinely smoother overall training trajectory, without the sudden, visible jumps in behavior that can sometimes appear right at a step decay schedule's own discrete drop points.
6. Cosine Annealing

blocks.alt: The learning rate follows a cosine curve down

blocks.text: A genuinely popular, modern approach is cosine annealing, reducing the learning rate following a smooth, cosine-shaped curve, starting high and ending genuinely close to zero, over the course of one complete training run.

This produces a genuinely gentle, gradually accelerating decay shape, distinct from both step decay's sudden jumps and exponential decay's constant proportional reduction, and has become a genuinely widely used, common default in many modern training setups.

blocks.content: Cosine annealing has become a genuinely widely used default in many modern training setups, particularly common when training the large architectures covered later in this course, given its smooth, gradual decay shape.

blocks.text: 7. A Related Technique: Warmup

blocks.alt: Training starts with a low learning rate, then ramps up gradually

blocks.text: A genuinely important, related technique is learning rate warmup: starting with a genuinely small learning rate, gradually increasing it over the first several epochs, before beginning the actual decay schedule already covered throughout this topic.

This is especially important for Transformers, covered in their own dedicated module later in this course, where training can genuinely become unstable if it starts immediately with a large learning rate, before the network's own weights have had any chance to settle into a genuinely reasonable starting configuration.
8. Interaction With Adaptive Optimizers

This connects back to Adam and its own per-weight adaptive rate, already covered fully in its own dedicated topic. Even adaptive optimizers genuinely still benefit from an overall schedule too, despite already adjusting each individual weight's own effective rate internally.

The base learning rate they adapt from can itself still usefully decay over time, meaning Learning Rate Scheduling and per-weight adaptive optimization, already covered throughout much of this module, are genuinely complementary techniques, not competing or redundant alternatives.
9. Recognizing When Scheduling Is Genuinely Worth Adding

blocks.alt: Training unstable or plateauing points toward adding a learning rate schedule

blocks.text: Essentially any real, extended training run genuinely benefits from adding Learning Rate Scheduling, already covered throughout this topic, a genuinely low-cost, commonly beneficial addition on top of whatever optimizer, from the earlier topics in this module, is already being used.

This makes Learning Rate Scheduling one of the most broadly, generally applicable techniques covered throughout this entire module, worth considering as a near-default addition to essentially any real, practical training setup, rather than a specialized, situational technique.

blocks.text: 11. Backpropagation & Optimization: Module Recap

items: Learning Rate Scheduling adjusts the learning rate over the course of training, applicable on top of any optimizer.
A fixed rate faces a genuine tension: too large prevents fine late convergence, too small causes slow early progress.
The core idea: start large for fast, coarse early progress, then gradually shrink for fine, precise late refinement.
Step decay reduces the rate by a fixed factor every fixed number of epochs, a simple, discrete schedule.
Exponential decay reduces the rate smoothly and continuously, avoiding step decay's sudden jumps.
Cosine annealing follows a smooth, cosine-shaped curve, a genuinely popular, widely used modern default.
Warmup starts small and ramps up before the actual decay schedule begins, especially important for Transformers.
Even adaptive optimizers like Adam still benefit from an overall schedule on their own base rate.

This closes Backpropagation & Optimization: from the chain rule through every optimizer to scheduling itself. Next module: Weight Initialization, covering where a network's weights actually start before any training begins.
